doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Fans turned producers, Riverside and Monk as guru
summary: Keepnews says fans like Lion, Gabler and Koenig became producers, how he became Riverside's creative director, and Rollins calling Monk a guru.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: exactly how I learned to swim. And it was, I also will say that, I said it many years ago with what I have learned I would never entrust as valuable and volatile a commodity as Thelonious to anybody as totally ignorant and inexperienced as I was at the time. But fortunately one of the great advantages of that, well basically it’s a 1950s phenomenon primarily, it happened a little before that, it happened a little after that, but the idea of the jazz fan as self-made jazz record producer actually the art owes a great deal to that phenomenon and a number of very important — Alfred Lion comes to mind, Milt Gabler, Lester Koenig at Contemporary Records. I don’t want to start naming names because you always leave out what you shouldn’t. But practically everybody, and it was very frequently exactly the same circumstances. If it was your company and you said you were the producer, there wasn’t anybody that was going to tell you you weren’t. So you did it. And most of us I must admit were self-appointed. Because I had a partner and Bill Grauer was initially a man, he was a serious jazz record collector and knew a hell of a lot more than I did about things but he naturally gravitated toward the business end of the company and so suddenly I found myself the creative director of Riverside Records and I made the most of it. The Monk experience taught me, quite seriously, not only how to behave in the presence of genius of a major artist, how to work effectively or hopefully effectively with somebody like that, and how to accomplish what you feel you have to accomplish in the face of who and what that artist is. And having survived Monk I have been fond of saying I could never again be frightened of any jazz musician. So it was, quite seriously, Sonny Rollins once in an interview with somebody, I think Stanley Crouch interviewed him at one point and Sonny, who of course during one of his sabbatical periods had spent some time in India, said that he thought that Monk was not a teacher so much as he was a guru, in the sense that a guru is somebody who enables you to bring out the best qualities in yourself. And Mr. Rollins, who is in addition to being an extremely articulate player, is also an extremely articulate thinker and expresser in words, this was a very specific point that Sonny was making and I think it’s incredibly accurate. Of course Monk has never had a student per se and never had. One of the true marks of an important person is that you will continue indefinitely to refer to them in the present tense. And I think that’s not just a slip. It may initially be that, but there are a lot of people — one of the glories of — thank God they invented the phonograph record. It keeps people very much alive. And unfortunately they haven’t worked out a way where they can vary what’s on the records, but in a sense we have with all of the emphasis on alternate takes that’s come about and the reissue scene. But these people are, the ones who remain a living presence, I still have that same attitude that combination of respect and veneration and pride, I do feel proud of what I have been able to help them to accomplish.
